Body Organization, Directions, and Word Parts

Unit 2: Anatomy, Physiology, and Medical Terminology. Lesson 4 of 53 in BMET Academy.

You will never diagnose anybody. You will still spend every day around people who describe the body in a particular vocabulary, and around devices named after the parts they watch. Learn the map and the word parts and the whole rest of the course reads easier.

How the body is built up

Four levels, smallest to largest:

  • Cells are the living building blocks.
  • Tissues are sheets or bundles of one kind of cell doing one job: lining, support, muscle, nerve.
  • Organs are structures built of several tissues with a purpose: heart, lungs, brain, kidney, skin.
  • Systems are groups of organs that work together.

The systems this course names are the circulatory system (heart, vessels, blood), the respiratory system (airway and lungs), the nervous system (brain, spinal cord, nerves), the digestive system (the tube from mouth to the other end, plus liver and pancreas), the urinary system (kidneys and bladder), the endocrine system (glands and hormones), the musculoskeletal system (the skeletal system of bones and joints plus the muscular system that moves them), the lymphatic system and the immune system it carries (lymph vessels, lymph nodes, spleen, white cells), and the skin, also called the integumentary system.

Systems do not work alone

A patient's oxygen number depends on all of them at once. The lungs load oxygen onto the blood, the heart pushes that blood to the tissues, the brainstem sets the breathing and the heart rate, the kidneys keep the fluid balance that gives the heart something to pump, and the skin is the surface your sensor sticks to. When a monitor shows a bad number, the cause can sit in any of those links, which is also why one patient is wired to several of your devices at once. Holding temperature, pressure, fluid, and chemistry inside a narrow band has a name, homeostasis, and most alarms announce either that the body has lost that balance or that the device helping it hold the balance has stopped.

Directions: the words on every label and report

anterior / posterior   front / back               the breastbone is anterior, the spine is posterior
superior / inferior    above / below              the head is superior to the chest
medial / lateral       toward / away from middle  the nose is medial, the ears are lateral
proximal / distal      near / far from the trunk  the elbow is proximal to the wrist
supine / prone         face up / face down        most patients on a table lie supine

These matter to you in practical ways: a probe placed more distal means farther out the limb, a cuff goes on the upper arm proximal to the elbow, and a patient lying prone changes where every cable can safely run.

Word parts: a decoder for terms you have never seen

Most medical words are a root (the body part) with a prefix (in front) or a suffix (on the end).

  • Prefixes: brady- slow, tachy- fast, hyper- high or too much, hypo- low or too little, a- and an- without, dys- difficult or painful.
  • Roots: cardio heart, pulmo and pneumo lung, nephro and reno kidney, neuro nerve, gastro stomach, derm skin, hemo blood.
  • Suffixes: -itis inflammation, -ectomy surgical removal, -oscopy looking inside, -graphy the process of recording, -gram the record itself, -emia a condition of the blood.

Assemble them and unfamiliar words decode themselves. Tachycardia is a fast heart. Hypoxemia is too little oxygen in the blood. Electrocardiography is the process that produces the electrocardiogram, which is why one of your devices is a recorder and its output is a strip of paper.

Exam tip: word-part questions are free points, so break the term in half before you look at the options. For direction questions, the trunk is the reference: proximal is toward it, distal is away from it.
Remember
Cells, tissues, organs, systems. Anterior front, posterior back, superior above, inferior below, medial toward the middle, lateral away, proximal near the trunk, distal far, supine face up, prone face down. Brady slow, tachy fast, hyper high, hypo low; -itis inflammation, -ectomy removal, -graphy the recording process, -gram the record, -emia in the blood.
Deeper explanation

Body Organization, Directions, and Word Parts, explained slowly

Why a technician learns anatomy

You will not treat anybody. You will read a work order that says "monitor alarming on a prone patient, lead placement suspect," talk to a nurse who says the cuff is on the wrong side because the arm is distal to a graft, and open a manual whose first page describes what the device measures physiologically. The vocabulary is the price of admission to those conversations.

Four levels, one example

Take the heart. The cells are muscle cells that contract when an electrical signal arrives. Bundled into tissue, they form the thick wall that can squeeze as one. Built into an organ, that wall becomes four chambers with valves. Joined with vessels and blood into a system, it circulates oxygen to every tissue in the body. Your ECG monitor listens at the cell level, your blood pressure cuff measures at the system level, and your defibrillator intervenes at the organ level. Same anatomy, three different devices, three different levels.

What to memorize

superior / inferior     above / below                head superior to chest
medial / lateral        toward / away from midline   nose medial, ears lateral
proximal / distal       near / far from the trunk    elbow proximal to wrist
supine / prone          face up / face down          most procedures are done supine

Prefix      Meaning        Suffix      Meaning

tachy-      fast           -ectomy     surgical removal
hyper-      high, too much -oscopy     looking inside
hypo-       low, too little -graphy    the process of recording

dys-        difficult      -emia       a condition of the blood

Root        Body part      Root        Body part

nephro      kidney         neuro       nerve
reno        kidney

Practice decoding

  • Bradycardia: brady (slow) + cardia (heart). A slow heart rate, under 60 beats per minute.
  • Hypoxemia: hypo (too little) + ox (oxygen) + emia (in the blood). Low blood oxygen, which is what a pulse oximeter is watching for.
  • Dyspnea: dys (difficult) + pnea (breathing). Trouble breathing.
  • Nephrology: nephro (kidney) + logy (study of). The specialty that runs the dialysis unit you will service.
  • Endoscopy: endo (within) + oscopy (looking inside). Looking inside with a scope, which is the department with the most expensive flexible cables in the hospital.

Where directions bite a technician

Three real examples. A pulse oximeter probe asked to go more distal goes farther out the limb, toward the fingertip, not toward the shoulder. A blood pressure cuff goes on the upper arm, proximal to the elbow, because the artery there runs deep and straight. And a patient turned prone for surgery has every cable, electrode, and probe relocated, because everything that was accessible on the front is now underneath them. Getting the word wrong in any of those produces a false reading or an unsafe setup, which is why the exam asks.
